Since \(\{n/10^k\}<1\), we need \(n/10^{10}<1\), so \(n<10^{10}\). Write \(n\) as a 10-digit string with leading zeros:
\[
S=s_1s_2\cdots s_{10}.
\]
Then
\[
\left\{\frac{n}{10^k}\right\}=0.s_{11-k}\cdots s_{10},\qquad \frac{n}{10^{10}}=0.s_1s_2\cdots s_{10}.
\]
So the condition becomes: for every \(k=1,\ldots,9\), the length-\(k\) suffix of \(S\) is lexicographically greater than the length-\(k\) prefix of \(S\). Equivalently, \(S\) is lexicographically smaller than every proper suffix of itself, i.e. \(S\) is a Lyndon word of length \(10\) over the alphabet \(\{0,1,\ldots,9\}\).

The number of Lyndon words of length \(m\) over \(q\) symbols is
\[
\frac1m\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)q^{m/d}.
\]
For \(m=10\), \(q=10\):
\[
\frac1{10}\left(10^{10}-10^5-10^2+10\right)
=\frac{9{,}999{,}899{,}910}{10}
=999{,}989{,}991.
\]
Thus the number of interesting numbers is
\[
\boxed{999989991}.
\]
